The 264-MW wind farm was completed in 2008, despite the legal challenges.

litigation_context: In 2018, Repsol Renewables North America began the development of the 650-MW Laramie Range Wind Project, comprising 170 wind turbines on approximately 56,000 acres 20 miles northwest of Cheyenne. The proposal faced strong local opposition, mostly from adjacent non-participating landowners. On September 16, 2025, after several weeks of public hearings, the Board of County Commissioners rejected the project with a 3-1 vote. During the public hearings, opponents of the project raised concerns about threats to wildlife, excessive noise, vibrations becoming a nuisance, obstruction of views and a decrease in property values. In November 2025, the developer sued the Laramie County Board of Commissioners in the Wyoming First Judicial Court challenging the rejection of the project on the basis that the county acted “arbitrarily and capriciously.”

project_name: Pioneer Wind Parks I and II
litigation_context: In 2011, Wasatch Wind proposed a 66-turbine wind farm in Converse County. The project was opposed by local residents due to concerns about potential impacts to scenery, recreation, property values, and the Laramie Range wilderness. The opponents formed the Northern Laramie Range Alliance (NLRA) to organize against the project, including by advocating for zoning regulations that would prohibit wind development above an elevation of 6,000 feet; when this failed, the group appealed state and county permitting decisions and eventually took a case to the Wyoming Supreme Court. Although these efforts failed, Converse County did enact slightly stricter wind regulations. Construction was completed in 2016.

litigation_context: In 2022, Focus Clean Energy proposed the “Pronghorn H2” project, comprising a roughly 300 MW wind farm and 280 MW solar farm, to power a hydrogen production facility. The project is to be located on public and private lands spanning a total of approximately 40,000 acres near Glenrock. The project has faced strong opposition from local ranchers, landowners, and a group called “Taxpayers Against Pronghorn H2 Project.” The opponents have raised concerns over public safety, water use, viewshed impacts, impacts on wildlife migration, and interference with private property rights. In April 2025, the Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners, in a 4-1 vote, approved a lease for the project. With the same vote, the Board also approved a lease for another project by the same developers in neighboring Niobrara County (see Sidewinder Wind). In July 2025, a local rancher filed a lawsuit in the district court challenging the state approval of the Pronghorn project. In December 2025, the district court ruled that the Board had violated its own rules by approving the lease for the project. In January 2026, the developer revised the project proposal, reducing its size to 30% of the initial footprint and indicating that it would move forward with only the wind and solar facilities and not the hydrogen production component of the project. In February 2026, the Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners, in a 3-2 vote, rescinded the land lease for the project. Chuck Gray, Wyoming Secretary of State and the only member of the Board of Land Commissioners to initially vote against the proposals, released a statement after the vote celebrating the cancellation of “woke wind leases.”

The Rail Tie Wind Project, a 26,000-acre, 504-MW wind farm proposed by ConnectGen (which was acquired by Repsol in March 2024), has experienced delays after becoming embroiled in legal controversies. At a meeting in February 2020, residents urged the county planning and zoning commission to place a moratorium on wind development to block the project, citing concerns about the potential for aesthetic changes to the classic western landscape, effects on local wildlife, and the potential for groundwater contamination during the installation of turbine foundations. An attorney representing landowners opposed to the project also lobbied the county to impose aggressive setback requirements that would effectively block wind energy projects. However, neither the moratorium nor the setbacks were implemented. While the State Board of Land Commissioners initially denied the developer’s lease application on 4,800 acres of state land in November 2020, the Board reversed its decision and approved the lease in January 2021. The Albany County Board of Commissioners then granted final approval in July 2021. Local residents and businesses challenged the permit, and, in May 2022, the Albany County district court upheld the permit. Over 45 residents signed onto an appeal to the Wyoming Supreme Court, and the Wyoming Supreme Court affirmed, upholding the permit on April 18, 2023. In December 2023, the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality’s Industrial Siting Council approved the project, drawing a lawsuit. On December 23, 2024, the Albany County Conservancy and other plaintiffs filed a lawsuit in federal court to stop the project, alleging violations of the NEPA, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act. The project, if completed, is expected to produce $130 million in tax revenues

litigation_context: The Rail Tie Wind Project, a 26,000-acre, 504-MW wind farm proposed by ConnectGen (which was acquired by Repsol in March 2024), has experienced delays after becoming embroiled in legal controversies. At a meeting in February 2020, residents urged the county planning and zoning commission to place a moratorium on wind development to block the project, citing concerns about the potential for aesthetic changes to the classic western landscape, effects on local wildlife, and the potential for groundwater contamination during the installation of turbine foundations. An attorney representing landowners opposed to the project also lobbied the county to impose aggressive setback requirements that would effectively block wind energy projects. However, neither the moratorium nor the setbacks were implemented. While the State Board of Land Commissioners initially denied the developer’s lease application on 4,800 acres of state land in November 2020, the Board reversed its decision and approved the lease in January 2021. The Albany County Board of Commissioners then granted final approval in July 2021. Local residents and businesses challenged the permit, and, in May 2022, the Albany County district court upheld the permit. Over 45 residents signed onto an appeal to the Wyoming Supreme Court, and the Wyoming Supreme Court affirmed, upholding the permit on April 18, 2023. In December 2023, the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality’s Industrial Siting Council approved the project, drawing a lawsuit. On December 23, 2024, the Albany County Conservancy and other plaintiffs filed a lawsuit in federal court to stop the project, alleging violations of the NEPA, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act. The project, if completed, is expected to produce $130 million in tax revenues

litigation_context: In 2025, Focus Clean Energy, Acciona, and Nordex Green Hydrogen jointly proposed the 1,000-MW Sidewinder H2 Wind farm on approximately 120,000 acres of private and public land in eastern Wyoming. The project has faced strong opposition from local ranchers, landowners, and a group called “Niobrara County Against Sidewinder” which maintains a website containing information and petitions opposing the project. Concerns about the project primarily relate to over public safety, water use, viewshed impacts, impacts on wildlife migration, and interference with private property rights. In April 2025, the Wyoming Board of Land Commissioners, in a 4-1 vote, approved a lease for the project. In July 2025, a local rancher filed a lawsuit in the district court challenging the state lease approval of another project by the same developers in neighboring Converse County. The district court ruled that the Board had violated its own rules by approving the lease for that project (see entry on Pronghorn Wind). In January 2026, the developers revised both the Sidewinder and the Pronghorn project proposals. In February 2026, the Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners, in a 3-2 vote, rescinded the land leases for the two projects. Chuck Gray, Wyoming Secretary of State and the only member of the Board of Land Commissioners to initially vote against the proposals, released a statement after the vote celebrating the cancellation of “woke wind leases.”

The developer Nature and People First has sought to develop a 6,000-MW, utility-scale pumped storage hydropower project on approximately 400 acres of land in Apache and Navajo Counties. In July 2023, three organizations submitted a letter to FERC attaching resolutions against the project from 18 Navajo Nation chapters and agencies. Nearby residents had expressed concerns about potential damage to underground water supplies and sacred lands, and that the developer had not sufficiently involved nearby residents. In February 2024, FERC denied applications for a preliminary permit for the project.
